opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to data and to the speed of iteration. In the digital world we have this enormous corpus of human knowledge, the internet, code, books, conversations, and we've learned how to compress it into these large models. On top of that, digital environments are cheap to simulate. If you want an agent to get better at writing software or navigating a browser, you can spin up millions of copies, let them try things, fail, get feedback, and learn, all in parallel and at almost no marginal cost. That's exactly the setting where reinforcement learning shines. It's what we saw with AlphaGo and AlphaZero: once you have a fast simulator and a clear signal, progress can be incredibly rapid.

Robotics is a very different story. The physical world doesn't run faster than real time, hardware breaks, every robot is slightly different, and collecting data is slow and expensive. We don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot actions and their consequences. Simulation helps, but the gap between sim and reality is still significant, especially for contact-rich manipulation where friction, deformable objects, and small errors really matter. So the feedback loop that drives learning is orders of magnitude slower.

There's also the hardware itself. Even with a perfect brain, you need bodies that are capable, reliable, safe, and cheap enough to deploy at scale, and that's a manufacturing and engineering challenge that moves on its own timescale, not the timescale of software.

I'm actually quite optimistic about robotics, and I think digital AGI will end up accelerating it, helping design better systems, write the control code, and generate synthetic data. But the order of operations seems pretty clear to me: we'll get very capable digital agents first, and the physical world will follow, maybe several years behind.

r001.rationale: The response says digital environments are cheap to simulate and agents can be run in parallel with feedback, while robotics faces the constraints of the physical world. This clearly attributes digital AGI’s expected earlier arrival to greater control over the digital environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think it really comes down to where the data is and how fast you can iterate. For digital AGI, the environment is already there. The internet is essentially a huge, pre-built training set, and on top of that you can generate as much synthetic experience as you want. A model can write code, run it, see the result, and try again millions of times a day. Every episode is cheap, it's fast, and it's perfectly reproducible. That's the setting where things like reinforcement learning really shine, because the loop between acting and getting feedback is so tight.

Robotics is a completely different story. The physical world doesn't give you that. You can't run a thousand copies of a robot in parallel in your lab and collect a year's worth of experience overnight. Hardware breaks, it's expensive, it's slow, and every lab has slightly different hardware, so the data doesn't transfer cleanly. We've had this problem for a long time, going back to the early work on Atari and then AlphaGo. The reason those worked was that we had a simulator that was the actual environment. In Go, the simulator is the game. In robotics, the simulator is an approximation, and the gap between simulation and reality is where most of the difficulty lives.

So my view is that we'll get systems that are extremely capable at reasoning, coding, maths, scientific work, essentially anything that happens on a screen, quite a bit before we have robots that can reliably do general tasks in a kitchen. I'm not saying robotics won't get there. I'm saying the digital side has a huge head start, because the whole economic machinery of the last decade, the compute, the data, the engineering, has been pointed at it. And once digital systems are good enough, they'll probably help us close the robotics gap too, by doing a lot of the design and simulation work themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says digital tasks run in a pre-built environment where actions and feedback are cheap, fast, and reproducible, while robotics lacks that control over physical experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how quickly you can learn from experience. In the digital world, you can run many experiments in parallel, and in some domains you can check automatically whether you succeeded. If you’re writing code, for example, you can execute it and run tests. That gives you a feedback loop that you can scale with compute.

In robotics, you have to interact with the physical world. You need hardware, things break, and collecting experience takes real time. You can use simulation, but then you have to make sure that what you learn transfers to the real world, with all its variation and uncertainty.

So even if the underlying intelligence is similar, the rate at which you can train and improve these systems is very different. That’s why I expect systems that can do a broad range of digital tasks to arrive well before robots that can do a similarly broad range of physical tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says digital experiments can be run in parallel, checked automatically, and improved through a feedback loop scaled with compute, while robotics depends on real-world interaction and experience. This conveys greater control over the digital environment as the reason digital AGI is expected earlier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that, in the digital world, you can learn and experiment much faster. You can run many copies of a system in parallel, give them tasks, and use the results to improve them. If something goes wrong, you can reset the environment and try again.

With robots, you have to interact with the physical world. Collecting experience takes time, hardware breaks, and mistakes can be costly. You also need to deal with all the variability of real environments. Simulation helps, but transferring what you learn in simulation to the real world is still a challenge.

So I expect systems to become very capable at digital tasks before they have the same breadth of capability in the physical world. That doesn’t mean robotics requires fundamentally different intelligence, but it has additional constraints that make progress slower.

r001.rationale: The response says digital systems can be run in parallel and their environments reset, while robots face physical-world variability and costly mistakes. This attributes faster digital progress to greater control over the digital environment.
